meta.title: Who really said "Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities because it is the quality which guarantees all others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Aristotle. Winston Churchill wrote it in a 1931 Collier’s profile of King Alfonso XIII, later reprinted in Great Contemporaries, echoing Samuel Johnson.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities because it is the quality which guarantees all others'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle — Winston Churchill wrote it in 1931 (in his King Alfonso XIII essay), building on a Samuel Johnson remark. The Aristotle credit is a modern myth.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — actually Winston Churchill
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Winston Churchill line, not Aristotle. He wrote it in his 1931 profile of Spain’s King Alfonso XIII — “Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others” — first published in Collier’s magazine (27 June 1931) and reprinted in Great Contemporaries (1937). The popular version drops Churchill’s own hedge “as has been said” and, since about 2010, has been widely mis-credited to Aristotle. Nothing like it appears in Aristotle’s writings.

source.heading: The real source
source.excerpt: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others. Courage, physical and moral, King Alfonso has proved on every occasion of personal danger or political stress.
trail: 1775 — the seed. Samuel Johnson tells Boswell that “courage is reckoned the greatest of all virtues; because, unless a man has that virtue, he has no security for preserving any other,” per Quote Investigator’s trace of Boswell’s Life of Johnson.

1931 — Churchill writes the line. In his essay on King Alfonso XIII, published in Collier’s, Churchill coins the polished modern wording, as documented by Quote Investigator and the International Churchill Society.

1952 — the streamlined line spreads. The polished modern wording first surfaces in print without attribution — in The Bernardsville News of New Jersey (27 March 1952) — and is only credited to Churchill in other US newspapers later that year, such as The Cincinnati Enquirer of Ohio (7 June 1952), per Quote Investigator.
By 2010 — the Aristotle myth. The line begins circulating online under Aristotle’s name (e.g. on Goodreads), a misattribution QI finds no basis for in Aristotle’s works.
source.excerptNote: Churchill’s own words, from his character sketch of King Alfonso XIII. Note the phrase “as has been said” — Churchill signalling he was echoing an earlier thought, most likely Samuel Johnson’s.

author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British Prime Minister, war leader & Nobel-laureate author
author.bio: Sir Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical and biographical writing. Beyond his speeches, he was a prolific author and journalist; his 1937 collection Great Contemporaries gathered magazine profiles of the era’s leaders — including the essay on King Alfonso XIII in which this reflection on courage appears.

misattribution.heading: How Aristotle got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is a genuine 20th-century Churchill sentence, but the internet has repackaged it as ancient Greek wisdom. Here is who really deserves the credit — and who doesn’t.

items.why: No such sentence exists in Aristotle’s works. The polished English phrasing is unmistakably Churchill’s 1931 wording; the Aristotle credit only appears online from roughly 2010 onward (e.g. on Goodreads), with no ancient source, as Quote Investigator documents.

Churchill actually wrote “…the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others.” The circulating version deletes his hedge — the very words in which he acknowledged he was echoing an earlier thinker, per QI.

Churchill’s “as has been said” most likely nods to Johnson’s remark, recorded by Boswell, that “courage is reckoned the greatest of all virtues; because, unless a man has that virtue, he has no security for preserving any other.” Johnson supplied the thought, not this phrasing (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: these are Winston Churchill’s words from 1931, echoing Samuel Johnson — not Aristotle, who never wrote anything of the kind, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Churchill placed courage at the base of every other virtue — a claim that carried extra weight coming from a man who would soon rally a nation under bombardment. He offered it not as abstract philosophy but as praise for a specific person, King Alfonso XIII of Spain, whose “physical and moral” courage he admired.
The sentence’s clean, aphoristic shape is exactly what makes it so quotable — and so easy to detach from its author and re-pin onto a more ancient-sounding name.
detailsBody: Churchill’s phrase “as has been said” is the tell. Decades earlier the idea had been voiced by Samuel Johnson, whose conversation Boswell preserved: courage matters most because without it no other virtue is safe.

Churchill didn’t claim originality for the thought — only for its memorable modern form. The irony is that a later age stripped away both his hedge and his name, and handed the whole thing to Aristotle.
